requirements.requirement: On node1, /tmp is mounted with noexec, nosuid, and nodev, and those settings survive reboot.
requirements.summary: Before reboot, /tmp was a tmpfs with all three required options and had a persistent fstab entry. After an acknowledged reboot and changed boot ID, the mount recovered with noexec,nosuid,nodev; execution and device access probes were denied.

requirements.requirement: On node1, /dev/shm is mounted with noexec, nosuid, and nodev, and those settings survive reboot.
requirements.summary: Before reboot, /dev/shm was a tmpfs with all three required options and had a persistent fstab entry. After the reboot, it recovered with noexec,nosuid,nodev; execution and device access probes were denied.

overall_summary: Both mount-hardening outcomes are satisfied, including persistence through a directly observed reboot. The mandatory restart protocol is strong: it records a healthy pre-restart state, acknowledgement, a different post-restart boot identity corroborated by lifecycle snapshots, and recovered system and mount behavior.
limitations: The nosuid property was verified directly through the live mount options before and after reboot, but no behavioral setuid execution probe was captured.
The final lifecycle inventory does not cover /etc, so the apparent retention of /etc/fstab.before-mount-hardening is inferred from its creation and the absence of a removal command.

operational_hygiene.summary: The mutations were narrowly connected to configuring, activating, validating, and reboot-testing the required mounts. Probe files and device nodes were removed, and the final snapshot showed no failed services, package damage, or new network exposure. One minor likely residue is the retained /etc/fstab.before-mount-hardening backup: it served as a safety backup but no later command removed it, so it appears to have remained after successful completion. No other unnecessary mutations were identified.
